explain.sub: Cardiology → Pulmonary embolism → D-dimer, subsegmental PE, Daniel score
explain.intro: Three diagnostic points around PE severity: how to read a D-dimer in older patients, what to do with a tiny clot, and how the ECG scores RV strain.
why: a

**Age × 10 µg/L (FEU) if above 50 years.** D-dimer rises with age, so a fixed 500 µg/L cut-off excludes few older patients; ADJUST-PE showed the age-adjusted cut-off safely rules out PE in more of them (only in low or intermediate clinical probability).
b

**Clinical surveillance, no anticoagulation (repeat leg ultrasound).** CHEST 2021 suggests surveillance over anticoagulation for isolated subsegmental PE with no proximal DVT and low recurrence risk; anticoagulate if cancer, immobility, poor reserve or a positive leg scan.
c

**Daniel ECG score: HR >100 = 2; incomplete RBBB = 2; complete RBBB = 3; T inversion in all of V1–V4 = 4; S1Q3T3 (complete) = 2; score ≥10 = severe pulmonary hypertension.** Each item reflects RV pressure overload; the full score also adds points for the depth of T inversion in each of V1–V3 and for each part of S1Q3T3, to a maximum of 21. A score ≥10 suggests systolic PA pressure above about 50 mmHg.
traps: “Anticoagulate every subsegmental PE”
Isolated, no DVT, low risk: surveillance (only 17% right).
decode: [pattern] HR 118, incomplete RBBB, T inversion V1–V4 — Daniel score?
[pattern] 70-year-old, low pretest probability — D-dimer cut-off?
explain.punch: Use an age × 10 µg/L D-dimer cut-off above 50, watch isolated low-risk subsegmental PE with repeat leg scans, and add the Daniel ECG points (tachycardia 2, RBBB 2 or 3, T inversion V1–V4 4) to grade RV strain.

steps.q:
**Give the five pillars of acute RV failure management, with their contents:**
a Maintain rate and rhythm
b Optimise preload
c Improve contractility and maintain perfusion
d Reduce afterload
e Mechanical circulatory support
steps.a:
**Pillar** | **Contents**
**Maintain rate and rhythm** | **HIGHER heart rate**; aim to maintain **sinus rhythm**; **cardioversion if new onset or instability**; **amiodarone ± DCCV**
**Optimise preload** | **UNDER-filled:** small fluid boluses **(50-100 mL)**, close attention to CVP; **OVER-filled:** diuresis with **loop diuretics**; **CVVH may be required**
**Improve contractility** | **Inodilators** (dobutamine, milrinone); **Vasopressors** (noradrenaline, vasopressin)
**Reduce afterload** | **Prevent hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis**; **reduce PEEP and airway pressures**; **avoid atelectasis**; inhaled pulmonary vasodilators; IV pulmonary vasodilators
**Mechanical support** | **IABP** • **ECMO** • **VAD**
bank_lines: DocT GT: In IPAH with acute RV failure on IV epoprostenol: never interrupt the prostacyclin (rebound PH crisis), optimise preload cautiously (loop diuretic, no aggressive diuresis), keep systemic BP up; CCB vasoreactivity trials are for stable outpatients only.

explain.sub: Cardiology → RV failure → Five pillars of acute management
explain.intro: Step 5 turns to treatment. Three Grand Test questions test it: a patient with IPAH on epoprostenol, and a patient with acute RV failure after mitral surgery.
why: a

**Maintain rate and rhythm: a higher heart rate; aim for sinus rhythm; cardioversion if new onset or unstable; amiodarone ± DCCV.** A dilated RV cannot raise its stroke volume, so output depends on rate; loss of the atrial kick in AF or block drops filling of a stiff RV sharply. Bradycardia and AF are both poorly tolerated.
b

**Optimise preload: under-filled, small boluses (50–100 mL) with close attention to CVP; over-filled, loop diuretics, CVVH if needed.** Most RV failure from raised afterload is over-filled; extra volume only dilates the RV and shifts the septum. In IPAH, decongest steadily, not by rapid aggressive diuresis that drops preload too far.
c

**Improve contractility and perfusion: inodilators (dobutamine, milrinone); vasopressors (noradrenaline, vasopressin).** Restore arterial pressure first so the RV coronary perfusion gradient returns (RVF-38). Vasopressin raises SVR with little effect on PVR.
d

**Reduce afterload: prevent hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis; reduce PEEP and airway pressures; avoid atelectasis; inhaled and IV pulmonary vasodilators.** Hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis all constrict pulmonary arterioles; high PEEP and plateau pressure compress alveolar vessels; atelectasis triggers hypoxic vasoconstriction. In a patient on IV epoprostenol, never interrupt the infusion: its half-life is minutes and stopping it causes a rebound PH crisis.
e
**Mechanical support: IABP, ECMO, VAD.** For refractory cases (RVF-43 to RVF-46).
mimic: Acute RV failure after mitral surgery vs LV failure
RV: dilated, hypokinetic RV, high CVP, preserved LV, hypoxia. LV: high PCWP, pulmonary oedema.
traps: “Aggressive fluids for hypotension with a dilated RV and high CVP”
The RV is already over-filled; fluid worsens interdependence. Start iNO (67–71% right).
“Increase PEEP to improve oxygenation”
Higher PEEP raises PVR and RV afterload.
“High-dose furosemide” as first step for hypotension
It drops preload in a shocked patient; treat the afterload first.
“Lifelong anticoagulation” as the right add-on in IPAH on epoprostenol (key; 64% right)

The key rests on older practice. ESC/ERS 2022 individualises anticoagulation in PAH (e.g. catheter-related thrombosis risk on IV epoprostenol). It is the least-wrong option here because digoxin is not routine, rapid diuresis harms and a CCB trial is only for stable outpatients; if ‘continue epoprostenol’ appears, choose that.
decode: IPAH on IV epoprostenol admitted with RV failure — most appropriate additional therapy? [DocT GT]
Keyed lifelong anticoagulation; disputed under ESC/ERS 2022.
Hypotension and hypoxia 3 h after mitral repair; dilated hypokinetic RV, preserved LV, high CVP — next step? [DocT GT, twice]
Start inhaled nitric oxide.
explain.punch: Keep the rate up and the rhythm sinus, fill only an under-filled RV and in small steps, raise arterial pressure first, and lower afterload with oxygen, CO₂ control, low PEEP and inhaled vasodilators.

steps.q:
**For RV preload, give:**
a The three principles of optimising RV preload
b The situation in which fluid boluses are carefully titrated
c The volume loading strategy, fluid and rate
d Whom volume loading is considered in
e Its three-part caveat
steps.a:
**Maintain adequate RV preload** • **carefully titrated fluid boluses** (in **RVMI, when afterload is NORMAL**) • **AVOID OVERDISTENSION**

 | **Volume loading**
**Strategy** | **Saline or Ringer lactate, >200 mL / 15-30 min**
**Use** | Decompensated RV failure with **NORMAL central venous pressure** and **LOW arterial pressure**
**Caveat** | Can **OVERDISTEND the ventricles**, **worsen ventricular interdependence**, and **REDUCE cardiac output**

explain.sub: Cardiology → RV failure → Preload and volume loading
explain.intro: Step 5 again: the fluid question, which turns on whether the RV afterload is normal. Two Marrow questions test the case where fluid is right: RV infarction.
why: a

**Maintain adequate RV preload, carefully titrated fluid boluses (in RV MI with normal afterload), avoid overdistension.** An infarcted RV facing a normal PVR behaves as a passive conduit: forward flow depends on RA pressure, so a fluid bolus raises output.
b
**Carefully titrated boluses in RV MI when afterload is normal.** With raised afterload (PH, PE, ARDS) the RV is already distended and fluid worsens it.
c
**Saline or Ringer’s lactate, >200 mL over 15–30 min.** This is a single, measured challenge with reassessment; RVF-36’s 50–100 mL boluses are the cautious steps for the RV with raised afterload.
d
**Decompensated RV failure with normal CVP and low arterial pressure.** A normal CVP in a hypotensive patient is the sign there is room to fill.
e

**It can overdistend the ventricles, worsen interdependence and reduce cardiac output.** Once CVP rises without a rise in output, stop: the RV is on the flat part of its curve. Nitrates and diuretics are avoided in RV infarction because they drop preload.
mimic: RV infarction vs pulmonary hypertension
RV infarction: normal PVR, fluid helps (with PCI). PH or PE: high PVR, fluid usually harms; offload instead.
traps: “Nitrates or diuretics for inferior STEMI with hypotension and clear lungs”
These drop preload; give a fluid bolus.
decode: Inferior STEMI, hypotension, clear lungs, normal LV — next step? [Marrow]
Normal saline bolus.
Inferior MI, proximal RCA thrombus — first treatment of hypotension? [Marrow]
IV fluids.
explain.punch: Fluid helps the RV only when afterload and CVP are normal, as in RV infarction; give a measured bolus and stop when CVP rises without a rise in output.

steps.q:
**For diuretics in RV failure, give:**
a The initial IV dose in patients NOT on oral diuretics
b The initial furosemide dose in those on chronic diuretic therapy
c Who IV loop diuretics are recommended for
d The two modes of administration
e What to add for resistant oedema
f The two caveats
steps.a:
a **Not on oral diuretics: initial dose 20-40 mg IV**
b **On chronic diuretic therapy: initial furosemide dose AT LEAST EQUIVALENT to the oral dose**
c **IV loop diuretics recommended for ALL patients admitted with signs/symptoms of fluid overload**
d Given as **intermittent boli OR continuous infusion**
e **Resistant oedema or insufficient response:** combine loop diuretic with a **thiazide-type diuretic or spironolactone**
f **Caveats: worsening renal function** and **HYPOKALAEMIA**

explain.sub: Cardiology → RV failure → Diuretics
explain.intro: Step 5 continues with the commoner situation, the over-filled RV, where removing volume lets the septum move back.
why: a
**Not on oral diuretics: 20–40 mg IV.** The furosemide starting dose of ESC heart failure guidelines.
b

**On chronic diuretics: initial furosemide dose at least equivalent to the oral dose.** ESC 2021 HF specifies 1–2 times the daily oral dose, because oral absorption of furosemide is about half and chronic users are diuretic-resistant.
c
**IV loop diuretics for all patients admitted with signs or symptoms of fluid overload.** Gut oedema slows oral absorption, so the IV route is used.
d
**Intermittent boluses or continuous infusion.** DOSE showed no clear difference between them.
e
**For resistant oedema: add a thiazide-type diuretic or spironolactone.** Sequential nephron blockade; distal tubules hypertrophy under chronic loop diuretics.
f
**Caveats: worsening renal function and hypokalaemia.** Hypokalaemia raises arrhythmia risk, which the RV tolerates poorly.
mimic: Over-filled vs under-filled RV
Over-filled (high CVP, distended RV, septal shift): diuretics or CVVH. Under-filled (low CVP, RV infarction): fluid.
traps: “The IV dose should be lower than the home oral dose”
It should be at least equal to it (ESC 2021: 1–2 times).
decode: [pattern] Patient on furosemide 80 mg orally, admitted with congestion — initial IV dose?
At least 80 mg IV (up to 160 mg).
explain.punch: Give IV furosemide 20–40 mg if naive or at least the home oral dose if not, by bolus or infusion, add a thiazide or spironolactone for resistance, and watch creatinine and potassium.

steps.q:
**For each agent give the dose, its properties, and its caveat:**
a Noradrenaline
b Dobutamine
c Levosimendan
steps.a:
**Agent** | **Properties and use** | **Caveats**
**Noradrenaline 0.2-1.0 mcg/kg/min** | ↑ **RV inotropy**, systemic BP; promotes **positive ventricular interactions**; **restores the CORONARY PERFUSION GRADIENT** | Excessive vasoconstriction may **worsen tissue perfusion**
**Dobutamine 2-20 mcg/kg/min** | ↑ **RV inotropy**, **LOWERS filling pressures** especially if **left heart failure** is present | May **aggravate arterial hypotension if used ALONE** without a vasopressor; may **trigger arrhythmias**
**Levosimendan 0.1-0.2 mcg/kg/min** | Combines **RV inotropy AND pulmonary vasodilation**; favourably affects **RV-arterial UNCOUPLING** | May aggravate arterial hypotension; may trigger arrhythmias
**Levosimendan bolus 6-12 mcg/kg over 10 min is OPTIONAL and NOT recommended if SBP <90 mmHg**; infusion may be decreased to 0.05 or increased to 0.2 mcg/kg/min

explain.sub: Cardiology → RV failure → Vasoactive drugs
explain.intro: Step 5 needs the three drugs used to support pressure and contractility, each with its own downside.
why: a

**Noradrenaline 0.2–1.0 µg/kg/min: raises RV inotropy and systemic BP, promotes positive ventricular interaction, restores the coronary perfusion gradient; excess vasoconstriction may worsen tissue perfusion.** α₁ effects raise aortic pressure more than PVR at usual doses and β₁ effects help contractility. A higher LV pressure pushes the septum back towards the RV.
b

**Dobutamine 2–20 µg/kg/min: raises RV inotropy and lowers filling pressures, especially with left heart failure; can worsen hypotension if used alone; can trigger arrhythmias.** β₂ vasodilation lowers SVR, so pair it with a vasopressor.
c

**Levosimendan 0.1–0.2 µg/kg/min: RV inotropy plus pulmonary vasodilation, improving RV–arterial coupling; may worsen hypotension and trigger arrhythmias. Bolus 6–12 µg/kg over 10 min is optional and not recommended if SBP <90 mmHg; infusion can go down to 0.05 or up to 0.2 µg/kg/min.** It sensitises troponin C to calcium and opens K-ATP channels in vascular muscle, which is why it lowers PVR and also SVR. No guideline names it the drug of choice; it is one option at step 5 after pressure is secured.
mimic: Dobutamine vs levosimendan
Dobutamine: β-agonist, short half-life, tachycardia. Levosimendan: calcium sensitiser with an active metabolite lasting days, more pulmonary vasodilation, more hypotension.
traps: “Levosimendan bolus in a patient with SBP 85”
Not recommended below SBP 90 mmHg.
decode: [pattern] Which drug combines RV inotropy with pulmonary vasodilation?
Levosimendan.
explain.punch: Noradrenaline restores the coronary perfusion gradient, dobutamine adds contractility but needs a vasopressor beside it, and levosimendan adds pulmonary vasodilation at the cost of hypotension.

steps.q:
**Compare inhaled prostaglandins and inhaled nitric oxide on:**
a What each reduces
b Where the effect occurs
c Effects on V/Q matching and RVEF
d Adverse effects
e Dosing
steps.a:
| **Inhaled prostaglandins** | **Inhaled nitric oxide**
**Reduces** | **PVR, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction**, and **SYSTEMIC vascular resistance** | **PVR ONLY at WELL-VENTILATED lung zones**
**Effects** | — | **Improves V/Q matching** and **RV EJECTION FRACTION**
**Adverse** | **Hypotension and HYPOXIA** | —
**Dose** | — | **Start 5 ppm; overall 20-40 ppm**
bank_lines: Marrow: Abrupt withdrawal of inhaled NO causes rebound pulmonary hypertension and hypoxaemia (endogenous NO synthase is suppressed): restart it and wean slowly, stepping down to 1 ppm before stopping.

explain.sub: Cardiology → RV failure → Inhaled vasodilators
explain.intro: Step 5 ends with offloading the RV through the airway. Four real questions test inhaled NO: when to start it, what it does, and what happens if it is stopped suddenly.
why: a

**Inhaled prostaglandins reduce PVR, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and systemic vascular resistance; iNO reduces PVR only in well-ventilated lung zones.** NO diffuses into the vessel wall, raises cGMP and is inactivated by haemoglobin within seconds, so it never reaches the systemic circulation. Prostacyclin raises cAMP and has a longer half-life, so some spills over into the systemic circulation.
b
**iNO acts only where ventilation reaches.** Blood is redirected to ventilated alveoli, so shunt falls and oxygenation improves.
c
**iNO improves V/Q matching and RV ejection fraction.** Lower PVR is lower RV afterload, so the RV empties better, and the improved V/Q matching raises PaO₂.
d

**Prostaglandins: hypotension and hypoxia.** These are mainly effects of IV prostacyclin, which dilates the whole pulmonary bed (including unventilated units, releasing hypoxic vasoconstriction) and the systemic bed. Inhaled prostacyclin is much more selective and usually improves oxygenation like iNO, with mild hypotension at most. iNO has its own harms: rebound PH and hypoxaemia if stopped suddenly (endogenous NO synthase is suppressed), methaemoglobinaemia, NO₂ formation, and pulmonary oedema if LV filling pressure is high.
e
**iNO: start at 5 ppm, overall 20–40 ppm.** Benefit plateaus around 20 ppm. To stop, wean in steps down to about 1 ppm before switching off; if rebound occurs, restart and wean more slowly.
mimic: Inhaled vs IV pulmonary vasodilators
Inhaled: selective for ventilated lung, oxygenation improves, little hypotension. IV: dilate everything, so hypotension and worse V/Q.
traps: “Increase IV fluids” or “increase PEEP” for RV failure after mitral repair (one in three chose wrong)
The RV is dilated and the CVP high; start iNO to lower PVR.
“iNO raises systemic blood pressure” or “improves surfactant”
Its goal is to reduce PVR (95% right); any rise in BP is indirect.
“Hypoxia after stopping iNO — give 100% oxygen and wait”
Restart iNO and wean slowly.
decode: Hypotension and hypoxia 3 h after mitral repair; dilated RV, preserved LV, high CVP — next step? [DocT GT, twice]
Inhaled nitric oxide.
Severe RV failure after PE, iNO started — primary goal? [DocT GT]
Reduce PVR.
Rebound hypoxia and PH after stopping iNO — management? [Marrow]
Restart iNO and wean slowly.
explain.punch: iNO lowers PVR only where the lung is ventilated, so it unloads the RV and improves oxygenation without hypotension; stop it slowly, because sudden withdrawal causes rebound PH and hypoxaemia.

steps.q:
**For mechanical circulatory support in RV failure, give the properties and caveats of:**
a ECMO / ECLS
b Percutaneous catheter-mounted micro-axial pumps
c Paracorporeal RVADs
steps.a:
**Strategy** | **Properties and use** | **Caveats**
**ECMO / ECLS** | **SHORT-TERM support, RAPID**; **oxygenator can be added** | Complications with use over longer periods **(>5-10 days)**
**Percutaneous micro-axial pumps** | **Limited pump capacity**; **ECLS preferred in severe cardiogenic shock** or where **high pump flow** is required | —
**Paracorporeal RVADs** | **LONGER-term use** (weeks or months); can be **combined with oxygenators** when pulmonary support is also needed | —

explain.sub: Cardiology → RV failure → Mechanical support options
explain.intro: Step 6 is mechanical support when drugs have failed. The options differ in how long they can run and whether they oxygenate.
why: a

**ECMO/ECLS: short-term, rapid; an oxygenator is part of it; complications rise beyond 5–10 days.** It can be placed at the bedside and supports both circulation and gas exchange; bleeding, thrombosis, limb ischaemia and infection accumulate with time.
b
**Percutaneous micro-axial pumps: limited pump capacity; ECLS preferred in severe cardiogenic shock or when high flow is needed.** They give about 4 L/min and no gas exchange.
c
**Paracorporeal RVADs: longer-term (weeks or months); can be combined with oxygenators.** Surgically placed, usually RA or RV to PA, for bridge to recovery or transplant.
mimic: ECMO vs RVAD
ECMO: fast, oxygenates, days. RVAD: surgical, weeks to months, needs an added oxygenator for gas exchange.
traps: “A micro-axial pump also oxygenates”
Only ECMO, or an RVAD with an oxygenator, supports gas exchange.
decode: [pattern] Refractory RV failure with severe hypoxaemia — which support?
VA ECMO (or an RVAD with an oxygenator).
explain.punch: ECMO is the fast, short-term option that also oxygenates, micro-axial pumps give limited flow without gas exchange, and surgical RVADs run for weeks to months.

steps.q:
**For mechanical circulatory support, give:**
a The five indications
b The three contraindications
steps.a:
**Indications** | **Contraindications**
**Primary graft failure following heart transplantation** | **Advanced age**
**RV failure following LVAD** | **Multiple co-morbidities**
**INFERIOR myocardial infarction** | **Irreversible organ injuries**
**Post-cardiotomy cardiogenic shock** | 
**Pulmonary embolus** |
bank_lines: DocT GT: Shock within hours of heart transplant = primary graft dysfunction (long ischaemic time), RV failure against the recipient's pulmonary hypertension, or tamponade from mediastinal bleeding. Acute cellular rejection takes days to weeks; only hyperacute antibody-mediated rejection strikes within minutes to hours.

explain.sub: Cardiology → RV failure → Indications for mechanical support
explain.intro: The deck ends with who should get mechanical support. The one real question, a shocked patient hours after heart transplant, was got right by only 23%.
why: a

**Indications: primary graft failure after heart transplant, RV failure after LVAD, inferior MI, post-cardiotomy shock, pulmonary embolus.** All are acute RV failures that may recover. After transplant the new RV, not used to pulmonary hypertension and injured by ischaemia–reperfusion, meets the recipient’s raised PVR. After an LVAD, increased venous return and a septum pulled leftwards overload the RV. Inferior MI comes from the RCA, which supplies the RV.
b
**Contraindications: advanced age, multiple co-morbidities, irreversible organ injury.** Support is a bridge; without a way out (recovery, transplant or durable device) it only prolongs dying.
mimic: Primary graft dysfunction vs rejection
Primary graft dysfunction: within 24 hours, ischaemia–reperfusion injury. Acute cellular rejection: T-cell mediated, after days to weeks.
traps: “Acute on chronic PH” or “tamponade” as least likely early after transplant (77% chose wrong)
Both are common early causes; T-cell rejection is the least likely because it takes days to weeks.
decode: Shock hours after heart transplant, ischaemic time 4 h, CVP 18, on iNO — least likely cause? [DocT GT]
T-lymphocyte-mediated (acute cellular) rejection.
explain.punch: Mechanical support is for reversible acute RV failure: graft failure, RV failure after LVAD, RV infarction, post-cardiotomy shock and PE; in the first hours after transplant, think graft dysfunction, PH and tamponade, not T-cell rejection.
